body: Venues book 6–10 weeks out. The show you want in September is an email you send in July — today's outreach is always for the calendar after next.
Breweries buy atmosphere, not tickets. Pitch them three hours of the room feeling good on a Saturday — not your press kit's streaming numbers.
Listening rooms buy the opposite: songs and stories. For those, lead with the EP, the writing, and one line about what the set feels like in a quiet room.
Coffee shops book on reliability. Mention you bring your own PA (if you do) and that you've never missed a load-in — logistics ARE the pitch at that tier.
A venue that hasn't replied isn't a no. The engine follows up monthly for three touches — most yeses in small-venue booking land on touch two or three.
When a venue replies with anything human at all, the robot steps back and it's your show. Reply within 24 hours from your own Gmail — speed reads as professionalism.
The one personalized sentence in each email is the whole game. Name their Tuesday open-mic, their patio, the band they had last month — proof you know their room.
Your draw is honest at this stage: friends, family, and whoever's already in the room. Sell venues the room experience and your promo work — never inflate a number they can check.
Every confirmed show is outreach ammo: 'We're playing X Brewery on the 14th' in the next email tells a similar venue you're already working rooms like theirs.
Wineries and event barns pay better than bars but book seasonally — spring for summer, summer for fall. When one shows up in the pipeline, move fast on the calendar math.
The follow-up that works isn't 'just checking in.' It's one new fact: a new single, a strong show, a video from last weekend's set. Give them a reason the second email exists.
A 'no' with a reason is a lead. 'We only book duos' or 'we're full till fall' tells you exactly what to send them in six months — note it before you archive it.
Farmers markets and community events book months out through a coordinator, not the venue inbox. One application form is often worth ten cold emails.
After every played show, ask one question before load-out: 'Want me back for a fall date?' The rebook conversation is 10× easier in person than by email.
Tag every venue in your show-week posts even before they've replied to anything. Venues watch who promotes — being visibly good at promo is a booking credential.
The pipeline's 60-day cooling period after three follow-ups isn't giving up — it's letting the inbox forget you were persistent so the next fresh cycle reads as new interest.
Your Facebook Events are booking evidence. A venue considering you will look — an Event with 30 RSVPs and photos from the last one answers the draw question for you.
Co-billed shows halve the draw pressure and double the room. If a venue hesitates on a solo booking, offer a split bill with an artist whose crowd overlaps yours.
Reply-positive venues that go quiet after scheduling talk aren't ghosting — they're busy. One cheerful nudge with two concrete date options usually closes it.
The EPK link belongs in email two, not email one. First email earns the click with one paragraph and one video link; the full kit is for the venue that's already curious.
Book the slow months hardest. January–February venues are staring at empty calendars — the same email that gets ignored in June gets answered in January.
One video answers 80% of what a talent buyer needs: you, live, one song, decent sound. Front-load that link — nobody books from a bio paragraph.
Categories in the pipeline aren't labels, they're scripts. A brewery email and a listening-room email should never be the same email — check which template a prospect gets.
Private events (weddings, parties, corporate) pay 3–5× venue rates for the same set. One 'available for private events' line on the site and in the EPK keeps that door open.
The best time to email a venue is Tuesday–Thursday morning. Monday they're digging out; Friday they're running a weekend. Same message, different day, different odds.
When a venue says yes, confirm four things in one email: date, load-in time, set length, money. Every back-and-forth after the yes is a chance for the gig to wobble.
Keep a 'venues I've played' line in the outreach signature once it's three names long. Peer rooms trust peer rooms more than they trust any pitch.
If two venues in the same town are in the pipeline, stagger them a cycle apart. Small-town bookers talk — two identical emails the same week reads as a blast.
A venue's Instagram tells you what they book before their inbox does. Thirty seconds on their grid — solo acts or full bands, originals or covers — saves a wasted cycle.
Ask every yes-venue what nights they're trying to fill. 'Whatever's hardest for you to book' has landed more residencies than any pitch deck.
The reply that needs you most is the lukewarm one — 'maybe in the fall' dies unless you calendar it. Note the month; the engine's next cycle is your excuse to resurface exactly then.
Openers get booked by headliners as often as by venues. The Front Range acts one tier up from you — their gigs are your warmest booking channel after the pipeline itself.
Every email the engine sends is from your address, in your voice. Read one a month end-to-end — if a line makes you wince, fix the template, because venues are reading it as you.
Don't discount to close a first booking. Play the fair rate or play a shorter set — a venue that got you cheap once will expect you cheap forever.
The merch table is part of the pitch for rooms without a budget: 'no fee, I keep merch and tips' gets a first date in doors that 'what's your budget' closes.
A thank-you email the morning after a show, with one photo of the full room attached, is the cheapest rebook insurance that exists. Two sentences. Send it before noon.
Holiday season books in September. If December matters to you — and December private events pay best — the pipeline should be working those asks by Labor Day.
The pipeline's job is at-bats, not yeses. Ten fresh prospects a cycle beats agonizing over the perfect email to two — reply rates at this tier are a volume game with a quality floor.
When a room is wrong for you — metal bar, DJ club — mark it and move on without sending. A clean pipeline of right-fit rooms outperforms a big pipeline of maybes.
Sound check the money conversation: 'What does the night usually pay?' is a fine, professional question in the first reply. Venues respect artists who ask plainly.
Your positive-reply list is your win list — it's the venues where a human said yes to you. When a new room asks 'where have you played,' that list is the answer, verbatim.
If the calendar's ever empty, play the free rooms on purpose: open mics at venues you want, songwriter rounds, brewery Sundays. Being seen in the room beats emailing it.
